item.title: Resilience as a governing principle in water governance
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01972-y

Water governance often treats resilience as an end state, achieved mainly through technocratic decision-making and standard engineering tools. Drawing on five international cases, we argue that resilience should instead guide governance design and operation through adaptability, coordination, learning and accountability.
item.dc:title: Resilience as a governing principle in water governance

item.title: Accounting for the mining industry’s global water footprint
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01945-1

Millions of people share rivers, aquifers and coastlines with mining operations, but years of regulation and voluntary schemes have left these communities with limited knowledge of what water is withdrawn, discharged or contaminated. De-risking the sector requires mandatory transparency, which should be made a condition of the capital now flowing into critical mineral supply chains.
item.dc:title: Accounting for the mining industry’s global water footprint
item.dc:creator: Tim T. Werner
Stephen Northey
Nadja Kunz
Masaharu Motoshita

item.title: Monitoring water attacks
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01952-2

Attacks on critical water infrastructure have become normalized in modern military conflict. To counter this, argues Hussam Hussein, water scientists must build and maintain real-time monitoring and documentation infrastructure in active conflict zones.
item.dc:title: Monitoring water attacks
item.dc:creator: Hussam Hussein

item.title: Water as our common denominator in the fragmented world
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01980-y

In the era of growing political polarization, water can be a force for cooperation towards a global agenda of unity, security, prosperity and sustainability, argues Kaveh Madani.
item.dc:title: Water as our common denominator in the fragmented world
item.dc:creator: Kaveh Madani

item.title: Confronting water bankruptcy
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-02002-7

With 2030 and the conclusion of the current round of Sustainable Development Goals on the horizon, the world has entered a state of water bankruptcy. A collection of opinion and research explores how this bankruptcy affects environmental and social systems and asks how we return to sustainable and resilient water futures.
item.dc:title: Confronting water bankruptcy

item.title: Sinking land is the fingerprint of global water bankruptcy
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01964-y

Land subsidence is the physical fingerprint of irreversible groundwater loss, yet remains absent from water governance. Embedding it as an early warning metric could help societies act before depletion becomes water bankruptcy.
item.dc:title: Sinking land is the fingerprint of global water bankruptcy

item.title: Educational bankruptcy in a water-insecure world
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01946-0

Engineers can enter the water sector through undergraduate engineering programmes that give limited attention to systems thinking, governance literacy and agency. Where these capabilities remain underdeveloped, the resulting mismatch constitutes an educational bankruptcy that can threaten water security.
item.dc:title: Educational bankruptcy in a water-insecure world
item.dc:creator: Isaac Wait

item.title: Global partnerships for saltwater intrusion
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01953-1

Saltwater intrusion is a global issue with local societal and environmental impacts. Global funding mechanisms will be key in finding place-based solutions.
item.dc:title: Global partnerships for saltwater intrusion
item.dc:creator: Pinki Mondal

item.title: Anode-free zinc batteries enabled by structurally robust solid–electrolyte interphase
item.content:encoded:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01993-7

Zinc metal batteries are sustainable, but deep cycling triggers a catastrophic structural collapse of the solid–electrolyte interphase. By retaining trace reserved zinc during stripping, this work prevents solid–electrolyte interphase degradation, enabling a 99.96% Coulombic efficiency and stable anode-free pouch cells.
item.dc:title: Anode-free zinc batteries enabled by structurally robust solid–electrolyte interphase
